preamble: Loss of the glottal stop [ʔ] is among the most frequent consonant deletions. In Vietnamese and Old Chinese the loss of a syllable-final *-ʔ left a phonemic pitch contour behind (Vietnamese sắc/nặng tones, Chinese shǎng 'rising' tone), a classic case of tonogenesis described by Haudricourt (1954). Elsewhere it is simple deletion: Proto-Polynesian *q [ʔ] vanished in Hawaiian and Māori, and Arabic hamza is lost with compensatory lengthening in most modern dialects.
phoneticEffects: Elision, Coda Loss, Tonogenesis, Compensatory Lengthening

examples.note: Loss of final *-ʔ produced the rising sắc/nặng tone series (Haudricourt 1954); cf. Proto-Austroasiatic *slaʔ.
Old Chinese final *-ʔ disappeared, leaving the rising (shǎng) tone; Baxter's X marks this tone.
Proto-Polynesian *q (a glottal stop) is lost outside Tongic; Tongan keeps ʻuta
Postvocalic hamza is lost with compensatory lengthening of the vowel; Gulf, Moroccan Arabic and Maltese (ras) show the same outcome.
